title: I built a full puzzle game in Godot with Claude Code and PixelLab, here's what worked and what didn't
author: Phil_PixLake
selftext: Deep Pressure is a digging puzzle where every rock you break puts pressure on its neighbours, cracked rocks collapse in chains, and if a chain hits the core you lose your cargo. Almost all the code was written by Claude Code, and what made that work was a headless board model plus 94 regression checks, so nothing goes in unless it passes. Balance I still decide myself, the AI only simulates and proposes numbers. Art was the weak spot, PixelLab gave me a great base rock but couldn't make consistent variants of it, so cracks and ores are drawn in code on top. How do you guys get consistent sprite variants out of AI tools?

comments.author: K_kkomi
comments.body:
The headless board model and 94 regression checks are really impressive. I'm also building games with Claude Code, and I've found that automated testing makes iteration much less stressful.

For the sprite consistency issue, have you tried using one base sprite as a fixed reference and generating variations from it rather than generating each variant independently? I'd imagine keeping the silhouette and proportions locked while changing only cracks, ores, and textures could help.

Really interesting project. The chain reaction mechanic sounds fun too!

replies.author: Phil_PixLake
replies.body: Thanks! That's actually what I tried first, I fed the base rock as a reference and asked for cracked and ore versions, but it either came back almost identical or turned into noise. So I ended up doing your idea by hand, the base stays locked and the cracks and ores are drawn in code as layers on top, which also lets them animate. What are you using for sprites in your Claude Code projects?

comments.author: ContDev
comments.body: the headless board model + regression tests is the part most people skip and then wonder why the ai keeps breaking stuff lol. for sprite variants i'd honestly stick with what you ended up doing, base sprite by hand and layer cracks/minerals in code, ai tools are still pretty bad at 'same thing but slightly different'. curious how you did balancing tho, do you let it simulate whole levels or just single chains?

replies.author: Phil_PixLake
replies.body: lol yeah the tests are what keep me sane tbh. Early on it was mostly me, I playtested a ton and tuned stuff by hand while steering Claude. Now it sims whole runs, not single chains. There's a dumb bot that plays full boards and decides to go deeper or cash out, a few hundred runs per setting, and I get a report with stuff like how deep it got and how often the core blew. Claude proposes the numbers off that and I sign off after going through it. The bot's kinda bad at the game tho so it's a vibe check, not gospel

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: Same experience here, the tools nail one sprite but drift on variants. What's worked for me is treating the base rock as the master and making variants as overlay layers in Aseprite (2-3 crack stages, a few ore clusters) on the exact same palette, so every combo matches automatically. If you draw them in code it's the same idea, just use the rock's own darkest color for cracks instead of pure black so they sit in the art.
